**The Art of Leaning Out the Window**

Lately I’ve been thinking about the strange value of the unaimed thought—the thought that doesn’t know what it’s for. We live in a time that asks every minute to justify itself. Even our rest is optimized: sleep tracked, walks measured, hobbies monetized, silence filled with podcasts. But there is another kind of attention, the kind that happens when you lean out a window just to see what the air is doing.

This kind of attention has no deliverable. It doesn’t convert to a skill or a takeaway. It’s closer to the way a cat watches a curtain move, or how a child stares at dust in a sunbeam without needing to name it. In that state, the mind is not empty. It’s full of small, unclassified things: the smell of rain on warm pavement, the particular blue of a distant hill, the memory of a sentence you heard once and never understood.

I suspect that this drifting is not the opposite of creative work but its hidden root. The best ideas often arrive after the conscious search has failed—when you’re in the shower, on a walk, staring at a ceiling. They come because you finally stopped asking for them. It’s as if the mind has a back room where it sorts the things you didn’t know you’d noticed, and it only opens the door when the front office is quiet.

We are taught to fear this drift. In school, daydreaming is a failure of attention. At work, a blank hour looks like laziness. But maybe what we call distraction is sometimes just attention that hasn’t found its object yet. The invention of the novel, the discovery of a theorem, the memory of a face—these are not produced by force. They are received by a mind that was willing to wander.

So here is my small defense of the useless hour. Not every thought needs to become a project. Not every walk needs to end in a step count. Some moments are worth having precisely because they don’t lead anywhere. They are like rooms in a house that no one enters often, but their existence makes the whole house feel larger.

And perhaps that is what it means to write freely: not to produce something impressive, but to let the mind move the way it moves when no one is watching—loosely, honestly, with sudden turns and long pauses. To lean out the window of language and see what’s there.

Today, the air through the window is cool and smells of wet leaves. A bird I can’t name lands on the wire, stays for three seconds, leaves. I watch it go. I have nothing to show for this. I’m grateful for that.
